demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
**Patient: Mr. A.**
**Age:** 62
**Occupation:** Stock Broker (retired)
**Therapy Session Notes – Week 4**

Mr. A. is a tall, dignified man who walks with a slight stoop, as if bracing against a wind only he can feel. He sits in the chair closest to the door, his hands resting flat on his thighs, palms down. He speaks in a measured, deliberate baritone, but his eyes often drift to the window, watching nothing.

He was a stock broker for thirty-seven years. He thrived on the chaos of the floor, the constant noise, the split-second decisions. "The market talks to you," he told me once. "It tells you when to hold, when to fold. You just have to listen." He retired three years ago, but the language of risk and reward still colors his world. He sees patterns in everything—in traffic, in the stock of his pantry, in the silences between his phone calls.

The trauma happened fifteen months ago. His only son, Kofi, a civil engineer, was returning from a project site in a neighboring country. There was a mudslide. The road collapsed. Mr. A. learned the news from a consular officer who called him at 6:47 AM. He remembers the precise time because he was watching the pre-market ticker on his iPad. The numbers were red. He was already calculating a loss.

He describes the moment as a "circuit breaker." The world didn't stop; it just went silent. He could see the officer's lips moving, but the sound was a low hum, like a server room going into emergency shutdown. He hung up the phone and went to his study. He closed the door. He did not cry. He sat at his desk and looked at a photograph of Kofi at his college graduation. He waited for the feeling to arrive. It never did.

For the first three months, Mr. A. functioned with what he calls "mechanical precision." He made the funeral arrangements. He called relatives in Ghana. He handled the estate. He did not miss a single detail. His ex-wife, Kofi's mother, was a wreck. He found her grief embarrassing, almost unprofessional. He told her, "Crying doesn't bring him back. We have work to do."

But the work was never done. Now, fifteen months later, Mr. A. is a prisoner of his own vigilance. He cannot sit still. He paces his apartment, checking the locks on the windows three times before bed. He no longer watches the news, but he reads the obituaries online every morning. He scans them for names he knows, for ages under forty. He calls it "risk assessment." He has stopped driving. "Every intersection is a potential collapse," he says. "Every bridge is a trapdoor."

He has not been to a grocery store in six months. He orders everything online, but he obsesses over the tracking numbers. He refreshes the page every few minutes, waiting for the delivery status to change. "If I don't watch it," he told me, "it will disappear. Things vanish when you aren't looking."

His sleep is a battlefield. He falls asleep easily, but he wakes at exactly 2:17 AM every night. He doesn't know why that time. He lies in the dark, his heart pounding, listening for the sound of a phone ringing. He has turned his phone to silent, but he still hears it. A phantom ring, a ghost in the machine. He checks his call log anyway. No missed calls.

He avoids his old colleagues. They want to talk about the market, about volatility. He cannot stomach it. "Volatility is just another word for uncertainty," he said, his voice flat. "And uncertainty is where people get hurt." He used to love the risk. Now he sees the downside in every trade, every relationship, every breath.

He told me last session, "I used to be able to read the tape. I could see the momentum. Now I only see the crash. I look at a stock that's up twenty percent, and I only see the day it will fall. I look at a person who smiles at me, and I only see the day they will leave or die."

He is not depressed. He is not sad. He is a watchman in a world that has already exploded, waiting for the next bomb to drop. He is waiting for the phone to ring. It never does. But he cannot stop listening.
